Myth check

Are last-minute flights cheaper?

Updated 2026-06-22 · 5 min read · Magellan Flights

There's a stubborn myth that airlines slash prices at the last second to fill empty seats. Mostly, the opposite is true — and believing it can cost you real money. But there's a real exception worth knowing. Here's the honest version.

Quick answer

Usually not. For most routes, last-minute flights are more expensive — airlines know late buyers (often business travelers) will pay up, so prices typically climb in the final two weeks. The exception: off-peak leisure routes with empty seats, where genuine last-minute deals occasionally appear.

Open the tracker →

The short answer

For the vast majority of trips, waiting until the last minute costs you more, not less. Prices usually rise sharply inside the final two weeks. The cheap last-minute flight is the exception, not the rule — and you have to know where to look.

Why prices usually rise, not fall

Airlines sell seats in price tiers (“fare buckets”). The cheap buckets sell first, so as a flight fills, only pricier seats remain. On top of that, the people still booking a week out are disproportionately business travelers on expense accounts — exactly the customer airlines charge the most. Dropping prices for them would leave money on the table, so they don't.

When last-minute <i>can</i> be cheap

The myth isn't completely empty. Genuine last-minute deals show up when:

  • It's an off-peak leisure route the airline is struggling to fill.
  • There's overcapacity — too many seats chasing too few travelers.
  • You're flexible on destination and can pounce on whatever drops.

That's exactly what our flight market surfaces — the routes trading below their normal price right now, from your airport.

How to play it if you must book late

  • Be flexible on dates and airports — flexibility is your only leverage late.
  • Watch a fare feed or set price alerts instead of searching one route over and over.
  • Fly mid-week — Tuesday and Wednesday departures stay cheaper even late.
  • Know your rights if a flight is cancelled or changed — see the DOT's aviation consumer protection office.

What our data shows

Across the 479 routes we track — and in the national fare data the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics publishes — the cheapest fares almost always belong to trips booked in the normal window, not the final scramble. When a real last-minute bargain does appear, it's because a specific route dropped below its normal range — which is the moment our tracker flags it.

Frequently asked questions

Do flight prices drop closer to departure?

Usually they rise, not drop. Cheap fare tiers sell out and late demand skews toward business travelers who pay more. Genuine last-minute drops are the exception.

When do last-minute flights get cheaper?

Mainly on off-peak leisure routes with unsold seats. If a flight is undersold close to departure, an airline may release cheaper fares — but it's not reliable.

What is the cheapest day to book a last-minute flight?

There's no magic day this late. Flexibility on your travel dates and airports matters far more than the day you buy.

Are same-day flights cheaper?

Rarely. Same-day fares are typically among the most expensive, aimed at travelers who have no choice but to fly now.
